doc.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015

chapter: Studio work in the rock and roll era
title: Itsy Bitsy hit and demos that became tracks
summary: Bucky recalls playing on a corny hit, never knowing which records would sell, and demos paying 30 dollars that were often used as the final track.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: All right, I’m going to try another tune on you here. I’m just going to give you —
[audio interlude]
Do you remember that one? You don’t remember it.
Who was it?
You told me that you played on this song.
Oh yeah, the Itsy Bitsy.
Okay so you do this date. I mean that’s kind of a corny song.
Yeah, yeah. That’s what the business was.

When you guys had a break, let’s say you had two hours, and I know you usually went into practice your acoustic guitar. But if you were hanging out in a bar or something, did you talk about this music?
No. No we never did. We didn’t even know what we did. And then when it came out it was a big hit, I said wow.
Isn’t that something.
And we did it every day. Every day. We made demos. The demos were what they used for a real track.
Right. They just were doing these scratch things and then they ended up using it.

Yeah, when the songwriters wrote the song we had to go do what they call a demo. It paid 30 bucks. And they give it to the publisher. The publisher would — say if the demo was real good they’d say to the arranger, “do it like this.”
Oh that is so interesting. It’s like backwards almost.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. And nine times out of ten they used the sound of the demo on the track.
Wow. Okay so then a couple of months later you hear this thing on the radio and you go, “gee that sounds familiar” and you’re playing on it. But you didn’t make any more money if a song became a hit.
No. We made nothing.
Wow. Ruth, do you remember like he might be in a car and Bucky might say, “oh I played on that?”
Once in a while. Not very often.
